observation_summary: A test expected a ClassCastException when adding a non-Comparable object to Frequency, but the code threw an IllegalArgumentException. The failing location is Frequency.addValue; the test expects the class to reject non-Comparable values at the boundary.
reasoning_summary: The fix adds a new overload addValue(Comparable<?>) and changes the deprecated addValue(Object) to delegate via a cast to Comparable. That changes the parameter contract / boundary behavior so non-Comparable values are rejected at the API boundary. This is an interface/contract-level correction (method signature/parameter type and call behavior) rather than a pure algorithm, guard, or assignment fix.
evidence_used: fix_diff_oracle unified_diff: added addValue((Comparable<?>) v) delegation and new addValue(Comparable<?> v) method
production_code_snippets Frequency.java lines 122-134 showing catch(ClassCastException) then throwing IllegalArgumentException
test_code_snippets FrequencyTest::testAddNonComparable expecting ClassCastException (comment and fail message)
evidence_gaps: No full view of other Frequency API methods (getCount/getPct/getCumFreq) in the diff to see holistic impact on interface
No explicit compilation-level or call-site effects outside tests (but test demonstrates expected behavior)

alternative_types.why_not_primary: The fix does not add or modify a conditional/null/bounds guard; it changes the method signature and delegates via a cast so the type contract is enforced at the boundary.
No assignments or initializations were changed; the change is about method parameter type/signature and delegation.
The internal counting algorithm/body was preserved; the change did not rewrite computation logic, only introduced an overload and delegation.
There is no concurrency, ordering, or synchronization change in the diff.
The bug fix does not correct associations among separate data structures or procedures; it changes the API boundary for input values.
The fix does not add a missing capability or redesign classes; it adjusts method signatures and enforces type expectations at the interface level.
